name: Introduction to Programming with Python
objectives: Using Google Colab in a web browser, open a notebook, write and run a print line, and read the last line of an error message, with the program running and any typo fixed using the error message
Given information a program needs, store it in variables of the right type, get input from the user and print it with an f-string, converting input to a number with float() or int() before doing math

Given a rule with two or more outcomes, write an if, elif and else block that chooses the right outcome, with correct comparison signs, colons and indentation, giving the right result for each test value
Given several values, create a list, add an item and read items by index, and use len() and sum() on it, with every index and result correct
Given a list or a task to repeat, write a for loop with a running total and a while loop that stops, with the total correct and no loop that runs forever

Given a small problem such as a budget check, write a function with parameters and a return value, call it in a full program and test it, with the program giving correct results for at least two different inputs

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Opening Google Colab and running your first line
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a Colab notebook, type a line of Python and run it.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Colab in a web browser, you will open a notebook, write and run a print line, and read the last line of an error message, with the program running and any typo fixed using the error message.
A program is a list of instructions a computer follows in order. Python is a programming language: a way of writing those instructions that people can read. It is used for websites, data, games, robots and AI.
Google Colab is a free website that runs Python in your browser. You do not install anything. Your work is saved as a notebook in your Google Drive. A notebook is made of cells: boxes where you type code and run it.
Your first instruction is print. print("Hello, world!") shows the words inside the quotes. The quotes tell Python this is text, not a command. If you make a typo, Python shows an error message. Read the last line of it: it tells you what went wrong.
Step by step:
- Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with a Google account.
- Choose to make a new notebook.
- Click inside the first code cell and type: print("Hello, world!")
- Press the play button next to the cell, or Shift + Enter, to run it.
- Read the output under the cell.
Words to know:
- Program: a list of instructions a computer follows in order.
- Python: a popular programming language that is easy to read.
- Notebook: a Colab file made of cells where you write and run code.
- Cell: one box in a notebook that holds code you can run.
- Error message: Python's note that something in your code is wrong; the last line says what.
Official sources:
- Google Colab: Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Open a new Colab notebook. In one cell, print your first name. In a second cell, print a sentence about your favorite food. Then remove one quote mark on purpose, run it, and read the error. Put the quote back and run it again.
You can now open Google Colab, write a print line, run it, and read an error message.

check.q: In a Colab notebook, what is a cell?
options: A box where you type code and run it
check.why: A notebook is made of cells where you type and run code.

check.q: You typed prnt("Hi") and Python shows a long error. What would you do?
options: Close Colab and start a new account
Ignore it and type more code
Read the last line of the error, then fix the spelling to print
check.why: The last line of the error tells you what went wrong, here a misspelled name.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Variables: giving data a name
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Store information in variables and ask the user for input.
This lesson builds toward: Given information a program needs, you will store it in variables of the right type, get input from the user and print it with an f-string, converting input to a number with float() or int() before doing math.
A variable is a name that holds a value, like a labeled box. name = "Maya" puts the text Maya in a box called name. hours = 20 puts the number 20 in a box called hours. The = sign means "store this", not "is equal to".
Values have types. Text in quotes is a string (str). Whole numbers are integers (int). Numbers with a decimal point are floats (float). The type matters: "5" + "5" gives "55", but 5 + 5 gives 10.
input() asks the person running the program to type something. It always gives back a string, so to do math you change it into a number: hours = float(input("Hours worked: ")).
An f-string mixes text and variables: print(f"Hi {name}, you worked {hours} hours.") The f before the quotes and the curly brackets do the work.
Step by step:
- Pick a short, clear variable name with no spaces (use_underscores).
- Store a value with =.
- For user input, use input("question: ").
- Wrap it in int() or float() if you need a number.
- Print the result with an f-string.
Words to know:
- Variable: a name that holds a value.
- String (str): text, written inside quotes.
- Integer (int): a whole number, like 7.
- Float: a number with a decimal point, like 7.5.
- input(): asks the user to type something and gives it back as a string.
- f-string: text starting with f that can show variables inside { }.
Try it now: Write a program that asks for the user's name and their hourly pay, and the hours they worked this week. Store each in a variable, multiply pay by hours, and print: Hi <name>, you earned <amount> this week.
You can now store values in variables, ask the user for input, change text to numbers, and print a clear result.

check.why: A number with a decimal point is a float.

check.q: You want the user to type their pay rate so you can multiply it by hours. Which line would you write?
check.why: input() gives a string, so float() turns it into a number you can do math with.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making decisions with if, elif and else
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write code that does different things depending on a condition.
This lesson builds toward: Given a rule with two or more outcomes, you will write an if, elif and else block that chooses the right outcome, with correct comparison signs, colons and indentation, giving the right result for each test value.
Programs make choices with if. A condition is a question that is True or False, such as hours > 40. If it is True, the indented lines under it run.
Comparison signs: == equal to (two equals signs), != not equal, > greater than, < less than, >= at least, <= at most. You can join conditions with and and or.
elif means "else if": a second check when the first is False. else runs when none of the checks were True. Indentation (four spaces) is how Python knows which lines belong to the if. Colab adds it for you after the colon.
Example: if score >= 90: print("A") elif score >= 80: print("B") else: print("Keep practicing"). Each part goes on its own line, with the print indented.
Step by step:
- Write if, then a condition, then a colon.
- Indent the lines that should run when it is True.
- Add elif for another check if needed.
- Add else for everything else.
- Test with values that hit every branch.
Words to know:
- Condition: a question whose answer is True or False.
- Boolean: the True or False type in Python.
- Indentation: spaces at the start of a line that show which block it belongs to.
- Branch: one of the paths an if statement can take.
Try it now: Write a program that asks for a temperature in Fahrenheit. If it is 85 or more, print "Hot: drink water." If it is 50 or more, print "Nice day." Otherwise print "Bring a jacket." Run it three times with 90, 50 and 30.
You can now write if, elif and else blocks and test every branch.

check.why: != means not equal to; == means equal to.

check.q: You want to print "Ticket free" if age is under 5 or at least 65. Which condition would you use?
check.why: or makes the condition True when either part is True; no age is both under 5 and at least 65.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Programs that repeat and remember

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Lists: keeping many values together
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a list, add to it, and read items from it.
This lesson builds toward: Given several values, you will create a list, add an item and read items by index, and use len() and sum() on it, with every index and result correct.
A list holds many values in order, inside square brackets: prices = [3.50, 12.00, 6.25]. A list can hold text too: chores = ["dishes", "laundry"].
Each item has a position number called an index. Python counts from 0, so prices[0] is the first item (3.50) and prices[-1] is the last.
Useful list tools: prices.append(4.99) adds an item to the end. len(prices) tells you how many items there are. sum(prices) adds up a list of numbers. "dishes" in chores is True if the item is in the list.
Step by step:
- Make a list with square brackets and commas.
- Read an item with list_name[index], starting at 0.
- Add with .append(value).
- Count items with len().
- Add up numbers with sum().
Words to know:
- List: an ordered group of values inside square brackets.
- Index: an item's position in a list, starting from 0.
- append: adds one item to the end of a list.
- len(): gives the number of items.
Try it now: Make a list of three things you need to buy, with their prices in a second list. Append one more item and price. Print how many items there are, the first item, and the total of the prices with sum().
You can now create a list, read items by index, add items and count or total them.

check.q: What is an index in a list?
options: The position number of an item, starting from 0
check.why: Each item has an index, and Python counts from 0.

check.q: chores = ["dishes", "laundry"]. You want to check if "laundry" is on the list. What would you type?
check.why: "laundry" in chores is True if the item is in the list.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Loops: repeating steps without retyping
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use a for loop to go through a list and a while loop to repeat until done.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list or a task to repeat, you will write a for loop with a running total and a while loop that stops, with the total correct and no loop that runs forever.
A loop repeats code. A for loop runs once for each item in a list: for price in prices: print(price). Each time around, the variable price holds the next item.
range() makes a list of numbers for counting: for i in range(5) runs five times with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
A running total is a common pattern: start total = 0 before the loop, then add total = total + price inside it (or total += price). After the loop, total holds the sum.
A while loop repeats as long as a condition is True, for example while answer != "done". Make sure something inside the loop changes the condition, or it will run forever. In Colab, press the stop button to end a loop that will not stop.
Step by step:
- Decide what repeats.
- For each item in a list, use: for item in my_list:
- Indent the code that repeats.
- For a total, set total = 0 before the loop and add inside it.
- For a while loop, make sure the condition can become False.
Words to know:
- Loop: code that repeats.
- for loop: repeats once for each item in a list or range.
- while loop: repeats as long as a condition is True.
- range(): makes a series of numbers, starting at 0 by default.
- Running total: a variable you keep adding to inside a loop.
Try it now: Write a while loop that keeps asking "Add a price (or type done): ". Append each number to a list. When the user types done, use a for loop and a running total to add the prices and print the total.
You can now repeat code with for and while loops and keep a running total.

check.why: range(4) counts from 0 and stops before 4.

check.q: Your loop adds prices but total keeps going back to 0 each time. Where would you move total = 0?
check.why: Set total = 0 once before the loop, then add to it inside.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Functions: packaging code you can reuse
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a function with inputs and a return value, then use it in a full program.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small problem such as a budget check, you will write a function with parameters and a return value, call it in a full program and test it, with the program giving correct results for at least two different inputs.
A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. You already used built-in ones: print(), len(), sum(). Now you will write your own with def.
def check_budget(prices, budget): starts a function with two parameters, the inputs it needs. Inside, you do the work. return sends a result back to whoever called it.
Calling the function runs it: result = check_budget([3.5, 12, 6.25], 25). A good function does one job and has a name that says what that job is.
Putting it together: the final task uses everything in this course. Plan it in plain words first (get budget, add prices, compare, print), then turn each line into code and test it with two budgets.
Step by step:
- Write the plan in plain words as comments starting with #.
- Start the function with def name(parameters):
- Indent the body; use a loop and an if inside.
- Use return to send back a result, or print inside.
- Call the function and test it with different inputs.
Words to know:
- Function: a named block of code you can run again and again.
- def: the word that starts a new function.
- Parameter: an input a function needs, named in its brackets.
- return: sends a value back from a function.
- Comment: a note in code starting with #; Python ignores it.
Try it now: Final task: write check_budget(prices, budget). Inside, use a loop to total the prices, then print the total and "Under budget by X" or "Over budget by X". Ask the user for the budget with float(input()), call the function with your shopping list, and test it with a high and a low budget.
You can now write and call your own function and combine variables, input, if, lists and loops in one working program.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Function There is no function, or it does not take prices and a budget. A function with parameters for the prices and the budget that returns or prints the result. The function has a clear name, does one job and uses return. Loop and total The total is wrong or no loop is used. A for loop adds the prices into a running total that starts at 0. Also prints how many items were checked using len(). Decision The program does not say Under budget or Over budget, or says the wrong one. if and else print the right message with the difference. Also handles exactly on budget with elif. Input The budget is not asked for, or is used as text so the math fails. input() asks for the budget and float() turns it into a number. Prints the result with an f-string that is easy to read. Testing The program was run once or not at all. Run with two different budgets, and both results are correct. Also tested with a budget that is exactly the total, or with an empty list. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What are parameters in a function?
check.why: Parameters, such as prices and budget, are the inputs a function needs.

check.q: Before writing the budget checker, what would you do first?
options: Plan it in plain words: get budget, add prices, compare, print
Type as much code as possible and hope it works
check.why: Planning in plain words first makes each line easy to turn into code.
